0.0.n: A casual, typically masculine way to refer to yourself.

0.1.n: Marks 僕 as the topic of the story.

0.2.n: Combines with 1年生 to specify the level of schooling.

0.3.n: Names a student's year in school, here the first year of university.

0.4.n: Links the student status to 時 to express when that status applied.

0.5.n: Follows 大学1年生の to mean the period when he was a first-year university student.

0.6.n: Marks the preceding phrase as the time when the event happened.

1.0.n: Refers to the university the speaker attended.

1.1.n: Links the university to the people associated with it.

1.2.n: Combines with たち to refer to a group, without specifying students or staff.

1.3.n: A suffix attached to 人 to make the group explicit.

1.4.n: Marks the people accompanying the speaker.

1.5.n: Pairs with に to describe doing an action alongside others.

1.6.n: Makes 一緒 describe how the speaker went, rather than naming a separate thing.

1.7.n: The Japanese name for the United Kingdom, rendered as England in the supplied translation.

1.8.n: Marks イギリス as the destination of 行く.

1.9.n: The plain form modifies 機会 directly: an opportunity to go.

1.10.n: The preceding phrase describes what the speaker had a chance to do.

1.11.n: Marks 機会 as what existed, naturally expressed in English as having an opportunity.

1.12.n: Polite past form of ある; literally says an opportunity existed.

2.0.n: A shortened まあ, used as a conversational pause before explaining.

2.2.n: The speaker continues using this casual, typically masculine self-reference.

2.3.n: Marks 僕 as the topic of the explanation that continues into the next line.

2.4.n: Combines with まで in 今まで, referring to the period leading up to this point.

2.5.n: Sets 今 as the endpoint, forming the expression 今まで.

2.6.n: Names the starting stage of the speaker's English education.

2.7.n: Marks 小学校 as the starting point of the schooling period.

2.8.n: A common shortened form of 高等学校.

2.9.n: Marks 高校 as the endpoint of the schooling period.

3.0.n: Names the language whose grammar and vocabulary the speaker studied.

3.1.n: Links 英語 to the grammar and vocabulary that follow.

3.2.n: One example of what the speaker studied, listed alongside 単語.

3.3.n: Lists examples rather than claiming these were the only things studied.

3.4.n: Literally refers to individual words; here it describes vocabulary studied at school.

3.5.n: Marks grammar and vocabulary as the things being studied.

3.6.n: Emphasizes continued study throughout the period, not necessarily without any breaks.

3.7.n: 勉強する in て-form plus きた shows study continuing from the past up to the point being discussed.

3.8.n: Presents the long history of study as the reason for the confidence described next.

4.0.n: Refers to the people around the speaker, likely his fellow travelers.

4.1.n: Marks みんな as the people receiving his comments.

4.2.n: Adds emphasis that he expressed his confidence to others too.

4.4.n: A very casual, masculine self-reference that sounds more assertive than 僕 here.

4.5.n: Marks 俺 as the topic inside the quoted speech.

4.6.n: With できる, describes ability in the language; casual speech leaves out が after 英語.

4.7.n: Expresses ability; 英語できる broadly means being capable in English, not only speaking.

4.8.n: Gives his claimed English ability as the reason others should rely on him.

4.9.n: 任せる plus ておく becomes a casual request in て-form, asking others to entrust things to him.

4.11.n: Casual form of という; introduces the quoted wording as an example of how he spoke.

4.12.n: Refers to the manner of speaking illustrated by the quotation.

4.13.n: Makes ふう describe how he was speaking.

4.14.n: Polite past of 言っている, describing ongoing or repeated remarks at that time.

0.lit: As for me, at the time of being a university first-year student,
0.tip: A noun plus の時に means when you were in that role or situation.

1.lit: There was an opportunity to go to Britain together with people from the university.
1.tip: 行く directly modifies 機会: Japanese puts the description before the noun, unlike English opportunity to go.

2.lit: Well, as for me, until now, from elementary school through high school,
2.tip: から marks a starting point, and まで marks an endpoint.

3.lit: Because I had been studying English grammar and vocabulary and such all along,
3.tip: てきた shows an activity continuing from the past up to the point being discussed.

4.lit: To everyone too, I was saying things like, I can use English, so leave it to me.
4.tip: っていうふうに introduces roughly how someone spoke, rather than insisting on an exact quotation.
